https://www.wgauradio.com/news/world/rus.text: Subscribe to WGAU newsletter(Opens a new window) WGAU facebook feed(Opens a new window) WGAU twitter feed(Opens a new window) WGAU instagram feed(Opens a new window) World UN health agency wants more details from Russia on suspected pneumonic plague case By JAMEY KEATEN, Associated Press October 07, 2026 at 5:31 pm EDT Enter Fullscreen Expand Russia Disease A woman with her child walks past the building of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, Russia, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. (AP Photo) (AP Photo/) By JAMEY KEATEN, Associated Press October 07, 2026 at 5:31 pm EDT GENEVA — A top official with the World Health Organization said Wednesday it doesn't know how a lab worker in Siberia died, and she urged Russia to provide more information about a case that prompted global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague . Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the U.N. health agency doesn't know what the "causative agent" was behind the woman's Oct. 2 death, which unconfirmed reports in Russia blamed on pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person. In its tersely worded statements, Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, does not link the case to pneumonic plague, saying only that the lab worker had contracted pneumonia of “unknown” origin and that “extensive” testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. “We don’t understand how she was infected,” Van Kerkhove said. “We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow-up of the questions that we have asked.” “We have posed these questions to our colleagues in the Russian Federation. In fairness, they have responded. We’ve gone back with more questions,” she said. The comments suggested the U.N. health agency has more questions than answers about the situation at the lab, which focuses on plague and was founded about a century ago to study the disease in Siberia, where it occurs naturally in wild animals. Russia has released little information about the case Russian authorities have kept a tight lid on information about the case, which has been surrounded by secrecy. While it has raised global concerns, Russian state TV and other national state-controlled media have largely steered clear of the subject. Some news outlets withdrew earlier reports about the case. Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday the lab worker was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” meaning its origin was not known. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported she died Oct. 2 in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk. Officials have quarantined that hospital and were monitoring the worker's contacts. Russia has said the pneumonia initially presented as a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection, the WHO has said, acknowledging that pneumonia is commonplace. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Russian authorities had indicated that no case of plague had recently been reported in the Irkutsk region, and that they had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine. Russia says preventive measures are underway U.S. President Donald Trump said he would discuss the issue during a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin because Wednesday is the Kremlin leader's 74th birthday. “They’re sharing it a little bit with our people. We expect them to share it a lot with our people,” Trump said. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier Wednesday that a Putin-Trump call hasn’t been set yet but could be organized quickly. Asked if the incident was a sign that plague might be developed as a bioweapon, Trump said, “We don’t think so. We’re going to find out soon enough, but we don’t think so.” When asked if the situation was similar to dealing with China on COVID-19 in his first term, Trump suggested Russia was staying relatively quiet, just as China did before the virus turned into a pandemic. “China didn’t say much and Russia is not saying much either, but they do say they have it very much under control,” he said. Dr. Erica Schwartz, director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said the threat to the U.S. “is extremely low.” She travel from that area of Russia to the U.S. each year is limited — and mostly comes through New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport. Government agencies are working “to make sure that we know exactly if anyone from that area comes into the United States,” Schwartz said during a Wall Street Journal health forum Wednesday. Russian health authorities reported a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing the dead woman’s contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests, the WHO said. The Geneva-based organization cited media reports that a second employee had pneumonia of undetermined cause. Health experts urge more Russian openness Peskov referred all questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which does not mention suspected plague in its reports and has not responded to a request for comment. In its latest statement Tuesday, the agency said “the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is calm.” Authorities were completing a “complex of prophylactic measures and medical observation over contacts,” it said, adding that so far they have found two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus. “No other infectious pathogens have been found among contacts,” it said. Judy Twigg, professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, noted that while the measures taken by Russian health authorities “have been swift and serious,” officials sought to play down the situation and “any statements that strayed from that party line ... were edited or deleted within hours.” “What we are watching is less a failure to respond than a failure of candor,” Twigg said in written comments. Vasily Vlassov, professor at the department of healthcare administration and economics at Russia’s Higher School of Economics, said the measures taken appeared “sensible,” focusing on treating the sick, isolating them and their contacts, looking for new cases and carrying out disinfection. He said it wasn't clear whether more transparency was possible if those dealing with the situation didn’t have enough certainty, and “maybe, they still don’t.” Deceiving the public, however, “always turns out to be harmful,” he said. Distrust of Russia’s official narrative is “natural” and “almost inevitable,” Vlassov said. In the Soviet era, dangerous outbreaks of infection had “a thick veil of secrecy — people were told nothing.” The lab worker who died was described as highly diligent The news outlet Lyudi Baikala — or “People of Baikal” — identified the dead lab worker as Darya Shipilova, 28, and said she first was hospitalized with cold symptoms Sept. 29 and died three days later. It quoted colleagues as saying she was a highly qualified and diligent researcher. They also emphasized that security rules at the facility are extremely strict. The report quoted Shipilova's neighbors as saying disinfection experts did several cleanups of her apartment, leaving a strong antiseptic smell. Shipilova’s mother, who worked as a doctor in the past, described her daughter as hard-working and dedicated, according to independent Russian news outlet Glubina, adding that she had not gotten official documents describing the cause of death. Twigg noted that Russia criminalized “false information” about threats to public safety in 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic, “so silence is the one safe move for everyone below the top.” “Personalist regimes without electoral accountability tend to treat bad news as a loyalty problem rather than focusing on the actual problem to be addressed,” she said. She warned that “the public’s understandable reaction to the lack of information carries real dangers.” “A government that is not believed when it says ‘there is no outbreak’ will not be believed when it must actually say ‘there is one; do the following.’ We saw this with COVID,” she said. Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague — also called the Black Death — are caused by the same bacteria, said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K. Pneumonic plague results from breathing in the bacteria, causing an infection in the lungs. The bacterium, called Yersinia pestis, has not been eliminated, but it is not spread very easily and it is treatable with antibiotics. __ Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, Collin Binkley in Washington, and Mike Stobbe in New York contributed. https://www.politico.eu/article/kremlin-.text: In September, a Russian court condemned a middle-aged man in Yaroslavl to 14 years in a penal colony — a sentence usually reserved for the country’s most twisted killers. His crime? Taking photographs of gravestones of Russian soldiers who died in Ukraine. With the Kremlin coy about battlefield casualty figures, independent journalists and activists have used photography to document the war’s true death toll, revealing losses far greater than Moscow has publicly acknowledged. “The multiplying number of graves — that must be a sight that’s bothering the authorities very much because it reminds them of the failure of Putin’s war,” Jan C. Behrends of the German-based Leibniz Centre for Contemporary History said. “So many people have died.” Advertisement Advertisement In recent months, Russian authorities have issued warnings that taking photographs of military graves could result in life imprisonment, while the Federal Security Service has patrolled the country’s cemeteries in search of offenders. Since the summer, several dozen people across Russia have been arrested. The official charge in these closed trials is treason — specifically, cooperation with Ukrainian intelligence services. Russia’s losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine are staggering. Russia 200 , a casualty-tracking database created by independent outlet Mediazona and the BBC’s Russian service, lists the names of nearly 283,000 dead soldiers, including details about the circumstances of their deaths. But Mediazona, which draws on open-source information like social media posts and reports in local media, does not have the resources and access to document every battlefield fatality. Other organizations estimate the death toll to be significantly higher. The U.K. Foreign Office and Dutch intelligence services estimate Russia’s losses to stand at more than half a million, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced in July that 700,000 Russian soldiers had died fighting in Ukraine. Even the most modest estimates of Russian losses in Ukraine far surpass Soviet casualties in Afghanistan, a conflict that lasted nearly a decade from its launch in 1979. Then, as now, the Kremlin strove to hide the true costs of war. Relatives of those who died in Afghanistan were forbidden from engraving the place of their loved ones’ deaths on their gravestones. “You could not mark the grave in any way that indicated that the person had died in the war,” Jeff Jones, a professor of history at the University of North Carolina, said. “Some [relatives] were actually forced to hold funerals at night so that it wouldn’t draw attention,” he added. Later, relatives were permitted to engrave the words, “died heroically while fulfilling an international duty,” but “died in Afghanistan” was never allowed. Advertisement Advertisement At the beginning of the war in Ukraine, the Kremlin wasn’t quite so guarded. In September 2022, six months after the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion, Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said 5,937 Russian soldiers had died in the conflict. Since then, there have been few official pronouncements about Russian casualties. As its “special military operation” turned into a protracted conflict, Moscow has ramped up efforts to conceal the numbers, shutting down new avenues of investigation for anyone trying to document casualty figures. In April 2024, a Kremlin spokesperson reminded journalists that information on casualties is a “state secret” and reporting on losses remains the “exclusive prerogative of the Ministry of Defense.” Sergei Shoigu attends the Victory Day military parade in Moscow on May 9, 2022. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images Later that year, Rosstat, Russia’s official statistical body, barred access to its data on the country’s excess death rate, which had been accessible since the 1990s as part of liberalization efforts under perestroika and glasnost . The Rosstat data was an invaluable source for verifying information on casualties — and for refuting government claims, says Dmitry Treshchanin, Mediazona editor and co-author of Russia 200. “We can count everyone name by name, but someone from government would always say ‘it’s fake,'” Treshchanin said. “But when you have official data confirming our calculations, nothing can be done with it.” Advertisement Advertisement Moscow has also stifled information on court cases concerning dead soldiers. In early 2025, Russian journalists noticed an unprecedented uptick in the number of court cases emerging about soldiers being declared missing in action or dead. Military units normally ask courts to declare soldiers dead when they do not return from a battlefield for months. “It was growing exponentially — it was big news,” Treshchanin said. “You start with 40,000 cases, then four months later you have 70,000, and two months after that, 90,000. I mean, just how many of these people could there possibly be?” Russia 200 recorded almost 90,000 such cases in 2025 — a more than tenfold increase compared to earlier years of the invasion. “And at some point, they just classified it,” Treshchanin said, referring to the government’s decision to restrict access to these court proceedings at the end of 2025. As for graveyard photography, Treshchanin and his colleagues are now cautious about using such methods. “Photos of graves and videos of the funerals were an important source of information for us at the very beginning of the Russian invasion, when not much other info was available,” he explained. But once the Kremlin got wise to the technique, it became too dangerous. “Our volunteers were attacked at the cemeteries,” he explained. The reason the Kremlin guards information about its losses so jealously is to more easily hire soldiers for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Ian Matveev, a Russian military analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny, said. Advertisement Advertisement “This is a way to deceive potential recruits. If people could easily find out what percentage of contract soldiers survive at the front — or how long a new recruit is likely to last — it would be extremely difficult to enlist even 30,000 troops per month,” Matveev said. By concealing losses, Moscow may also try to impress an “external audience — specifically, at Donald Trump — to convince him that Putin’s army is on the verge of winning the war,” he added. With each new restriction from the Kremlin, journalists are forced to adjust their methods. “Russia is big,” said Treshchanin. “If something gets stifled in one place, it means that, conversely, something else ends up growing elsewhere.”
